query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor tungsten (W) alloying addition to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will form fine, tungsten-rich precipitates at lamellar and grain boundaries that improve high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion stability while maintaining an acceptable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Add a small concentration (on the order of 1–2 at.%) of tungsten to the base alloy composition
generation.conditions: Testing under conditions that mimic aircraft/spacecraft service, including extreme temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loading (creep conditions), and corrosive environments
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, thermally stable tungsten-rich precipitates that segregate along lamellar interfaces and grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: W tungsten atoms, owing to their low diffusivity and high melting point, are expected to segregate and precipitate along interfaces during controlled cooling. These precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding (reducing creep rate) and can also hinder corrosive attack by stabilizing the microstructure under thermal and mechanical stress, while not excessively embrittling the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature strength and reduced creep rates along with enhanced corrosion resistance, with minimal compromise to ductility relative to the baseline alloy
generation.baseline: The current AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA without tungsten, which exhibits good strength and ductility but limited performance under prolonged high-temperature and corrosive conditions
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be beneficial primarily under high-temperature, high-stress, and corrosive environments typical of aerospace fastener applications; effects under ambient or mild conditions may be negligible or require separate evaluation
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement in creep resistance and corrosion stability is not precisely known; furthermore, the optimal tungsten concentration and processing conditions need refinement to balance the strength–ductility trade-off

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with the controlled tungsten addition (1–2 at.%). Subject both sets to accelerated high-temperature creep tests (e.g., constant load tests at service-relevant temperatures), cyclic thermal fluctuations, and corrosion tests in simulated aerospace environments. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM) for precipitate formation and perform mechanical tests (tensile, creep, and fracture toughness measurements).
measurements: Creep rate under sustained load at elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate in a controlled corrosive medium
Microstructural analyses (precipitate size, distribution, and interface characteristics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the tungsten-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in creep resistance or corrosion stability compared to the baseline, or if the addition of tungsten adversely impacts ductility or overall mechanical performance beyond acceptable limits for aerospace fastener applications.
